senses.definition: used before an uncountable noun, mainly in questions and negative sentences, to mean a large amount
senses.explanation: **Much** goes before an uncountable noun and is most natural in a question or a negative sentence: *how much time?*, *not much time*. In an ordinary positive statement, **a lot of** is the everyday choice (*I have a lot of time*); bare **much** there (*I have much time*) sounds formal or old-fashioned, though it is common after **so**, **too**, and **as**.

examples.text: How much time do we have left?
I don't have much money with me.
There isn't much traffic this early.
We spent too much time in the airport.

compare.note: **much** goes with an uncountable noun; **many** goes with a plural countable noun

usage_note: In an ordinary positive statement, **a lot of** is far more common than bare **much**: say *I have a lot of homework*, not *I have much homework*, which sounds stiff or literary. **Much** is completely normal in questions (*how much...?*), negatives (*not much...*), and after **so**, **too**, and **as**. The comparative of **much** is **more**, and the superlative is **most**, shared with **many**. **Much** used alone, without a following noun (*much has changed*), or as an adverb (*I don't like it much*), belongs to separate entries.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have much work to do today.
learner_errors.correct: I have a lot of work to do today.
learner_errors.note: In an everyday positive statement, **a lot of** is the natural choice; bare **much** there sounds formal.
An uncountable noun like **money** needs **much**, not **many**.

see_also.note: **much** used alone, without a following noun: *much has changed*
**much** used to modify a verb or adjective: *I don't like it much*

adaptation.grammar: **Much** goes only with an uncountable noun; the matching word for a plural countable noun is **many**. In ordinary positive statements, **a lot of** usually replaces bare **much**.
